title: The Pot Won't Dry
scene: The seedling is drooping even though the root zone is still wet. The room smells fine, but the container has stayed heavy far longer than expected.
lesson: A saturated root zone can reduce oxygen availability. Diagnose water status before adding more irrigation or fertilizer.

choices.label: Pause irrigation, improve air movement, and watch the dryback
choices.feedback: Good read. You treated the wet root zone as an aeration/water-management problem instead of adding another input.

choices.label: Add a stronger feed because the plant looks hungry
choices.feedback: The root zone was already saturated. More solution increases the load without correcting the underlying oxygen problem.

choices.label: Do nothing and check again much later
choices.feedback: Avoiding more water helps, but active observation and environmental correction would give the plant a better recovery path.

title: Top Growth Is Praying Too Hard
scene: The newest leaves are paling and curling upward near the center of the light footprint while lower growth still looks normal.
lesson: When symptoms are strongest nearest the fixture, verify light intensity and leaf temperature before assuming a nutrient problem.

choices.label: Check canopy conditions and reduce or raise the light if needed
choices.feedback: You matched the symptom pattern to the environment and changed the likely stressor instead of chasing nutrients.

choices.label: Add more light hours so the plant can recover faster
choices.feedback: More exposure can compound light and heat stress. Recovery starts with reducing the excessive demand.

choices.label: Increase nutrients immediately
choices.feedback: The location of the damage points to the canopy environment first. Feeding without diagnosis adds another variable.

title: Tiny Flyers at the Media Line
scene: You notice a few small dark flies staying close to moist substrate. The plant is still growing, but the population could expand quickly.
lesson: Integrated pest management starts with identification, monitoring, sanitation, and correcting conditions that favor the pest.

choices.label: Scout closely, add monitoring cards, clean debris, and correct excess surface moisture
choices.feedback: You used an IPM sequence: identify, monitor, remove favorable conditions, and gather evidence before escalating controls.

choices.label: Use a random strong spray before identifying the pest
choices.feedback: Unplanned treatment can stress the plant and still miss the pest. Identification and monitoring should drive the response.

choices.label: Ignore them because only a few are visible
choices.feedback: Early scouting is valuable precisely because populations are easier to manage before they become obvious.

title: The Meter Says Something Changed
scene: A root-zone reading is far from the previous trend, but the plant has only subtle symptoms and the meter has not been checked recently.
lesson: A surprising measurement should be verified before aggressive correction. Instrument error and sampling method can create false diagnoses.

choices.label: Verify the meter and repeat the measurement before changing the root zone
choices.feedback: You verified the evidence before acting. That prevents a bad reading from turning into a real root-zone problem.

choices.label: Make a large correction immediately
choices.feedback: Large reactive corrections can create instability. Confirm the measurement first, then make controlled changes if needed.

choices.label: Assume the reading is meaningless and stop checking
choices.feedback: Skepticism is useful, but the right response is verification—not abandoning measurement.

title: Stretching Toward the Fixture
scene: The seedling has a long flexible stem and leans easily when the room is disturbed.
lesson: Weak elongated growth is a reason to inspect light placement, airflow, support, and overall seedling conditions before using aggressive training.

choices.label: Stabilize the environment, add gentle air movement, and support the stem
choices.feedback: You supported the young plant while addressing environmental causes instead of treating a seedling like a mature training project.

choices.label: Bend and heavily train the seedling immediately
choices.feedback: Aggressive training adds stress before the young stem and root system are ready.

choices.label: Stake it upright but change nothing else
choices.feedback: Support helps prevent damage, but the underlying light or airflow issue still deserves attention.

title: The Room Swings Hard After Lights Out
scene: Day conditions are stable, but the room changes sharply when the lights cycle and growth has slowed.
lesson: Environmental stability matters. Before changing nutrition, inspect temperature, humidity, airflow, and the timing of those changes.

choices.label: Track the swing and stabilize the room before changing the feed
choices.feedback: You kept the diagnosis tied to the observed environmental change and reduced an unnecessary variable.

choices.label: Rewrite the nutrient program first
choices.feedback: The strongest clue was the environmental swing. Changing feed first makes the diagnosis harder.

choices.label: Ignore it because the daily average still looks acceptable
choices.feedback: Averages can hide stressful transitions. The timing and size of swings can matter even when the mean looks normal.

title: A Leaf Starts Losing Color
scene: One symptom appears: pale tissue. You do not yet know whether it began on old or new growth, and no root-zone measurements have been verified.
lesson: Visual symptoms are clues, not proof. A useful diagnosis combines symptom location and pattern with root-zone and environmental context.

choices.label: Map where the symptom started and verify root-zone/environment data
choices.feedback: You collected the context needed to distinguish several look-alike causes instead of treating color loss as a single diagnosis.

choices.label: Add a broad heavy nutrient dose immediately
choices.feedback: A broad correction without diagnosis can worsen the root zone and hide the original cause.

choices.label: Remove the leaf and call the problem solved
choices.feedback: Removing a symptom does not explain why it appeared. Track the pattern before the next decision.

title: The Next Container Is Waiting
scene: The plant has recovered well. Growth is active and the current root zone cycles predictably. You need to decide whether to move it forward.
lesson: Transplant timing should use plant/root development and container behavior rather than a calendar alone.

choices.label: Check root development and current container behavior, then transplant if ready
choices.feedback: You based the transition on plant readiness and root-zone behavior. The Seedling Shift is ready to close.

choices.label: Transplant only because the planned date arrived
choices.feedback: Schedules help organize work, but biological readiness is the stronger signal for the plant.

choices.label: Keep it in the small container indefinitely because it is currently healthy
choices.feedback: A plant can outgrow a stable small container. Healthy current conditions do not mean the root zone should never advance.
